Venice. A historic city-state built on lagoon islands in northeastern Italy, founded in the fifth century and rising to become a Mediterranean superpower during the Middle Ages and Renaissance. Once the heart of a maritime empire controlling crucial trade routes between Europe and the Orient, Venice developed a unique republican government and a cosmopolitan culture that shaped Renaissance art and thought.

Venice is built on one hundred eighteen small islands connected by approximately one hundred fifty canals and four hundred bridges, with no roads—a unique geographic adaptation that became its architectural identity. The Venetian Republic, from roughly seven hundred to seventeen ninety-seven, was one of history's most successful and longest-lasting republics, rivaling great powers and maintaining its independence for over a thousand years. It dominated Mediterranean trade, especially spice routes from the Middle East and Asia, accumulating immense wealth and becoming the hub of European-Oriental commerce.

Venice produced masterpieces of art and architecture during the Renaissance, including works by Titian, Tintoretto, and Paolo Veronese, with the Basilica di San Marco standing as an architectural crown jewel. The Doge, the Venetian chief executive, wielded power constrained by law and councils, making Venice a model of checks and balances that influenced later democratic theory. Venice was connected to mainland Italy via the Po Valley, whose territories fed and enriched the city. Control of Po-valley cities was critical to Venetian survival.

Venice declined as a superpower after the opening of Atlantic trade routes and European colonial expansion shifted economic power away from the Mediterranean in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, transforming it from a global power into a regional player.
